problem: Existing surveys cover traditional socially aware navigation, RL in social robotics broadly, or multi-agent DRL without social awareness. None jointly analyzes DRL algorithms and neural architectures for socially aware navigation (SAN) of mobile robots.
motivation: Robots increasingly share spaces with humans and must respect proxemics, comfort and naturalness. DRL can learn such behavior, but design choices (algorithm family, network architecture, reward, evaluation) are scattered, and evaluation is non-uniform. A unified taxonomy and comparison would guide practitioners and expose gaps.
key_idea: A survey of 100+ DRL-based SAN works that organizes them in a unified taxonomy by RL algorithm family (value-based, policy-based, actor-critic) and neural architecture (FFNN, CNN, RNN, GNN, Transformer), plus reward design, evaluation metrics, datasets, simulators and sim-to-real.
insight: The survey finds that value-based methods (DQN, deep V-learning) suit simple discrete scenarios but give rigid, jerky motion. Policy-based methods (PPO) give smoother motion, and actor-critic methods with GNN or Transformer encoders look most promising for complex multi-agent settings, at high compute cost. Metric analysis of the surveyed papers shows technical metrics dominate (success rate 65%, collision rate 57%) while social naturalness and smoothness metrics appear in under 2% of papers, so evaluation is non-standardized. Only about half of the works were deployed on real robots.
method: Literature search: Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore and Scopus, 2017–2025, using 'socially-aware/human-aware/crowd-aware' AND 'deep reinforcement learning' AND 'mobile robot'.

Algorithm taxonomy: value-based (Q-learning, DQN, deep V-learning), policy-based (PPO, TRPO, DPG) and actor-critic (A2C/A3C, DDPG, SAC, TD3). Comparison tables 2-4 score each work on comfort, naturalness, trajectory and intention prediction, attention, physical input, context awareness and advanced socialness.

Reward design and space analysis: covers collision, arrival, discomfort-distance, time, zone-entering, group, feature-based and progress rewards, plus trade-offs of continuous vs discrete state/action spaces and CTE/DTE/CTDE multi-robot paradigms.
Neural architecture taxonomy: FFNN, GNN (GCN/GAT), RNN (LSTM/GRU), CNN and Transformer, with application areas, strengths and weaknesses.

Evaluation review: navigation and social metrics with usage statistics, datasets (SCAND, ETH/UCY, THOR, SocNav1/2), simulators (CrowdNav, SocNavGym, iGibson, PedSimROS, Gazebo), benchmarks (SocNavBench, SEAN 2.0, SRPB), sim-to-real, and a proposed core metric set (PSC, TTC, clearance, smoothness).
Challenges and future directions: uncertainty, sim-to-real, compute, generalization, scalability, reproducibility.

setting.backbone: N/A (survey); reviews DRL policies with FFNN/CNN/RNN/GNN/Transformer
setting.observation: N/A (survey); covers LiDAR, relative positions and RGB in reviewed works
setting.action_space: N/A (survey); covers continuous and discrete velocity/heading actions
setting.simulator: N/A (survey); reviews CrowdNav/OpenAI Gym, SocNavGym, iGibson, PedSimROS, Gazebo

numbers_note: Survey paper with no experiments of its own. The only figures are literature statistics (e.g. success rate used in 65% of surveyed papers, collision rate 57%).
results: The comparative analysis concludes that DRL improves safety and human acceptance over traditional reactive and proactive methods. Actor-critic with graph or transformer encoders shows the most promise for real-world deployment. The field is limited by non-uniform evaluation, missing standardized social metrics, compute cost and the sim-to-real gap.
limitations: Qualitative review with no unified quantitative comparison of methods, since the surveyed papers use heterogeneous metrics and simulators.
Covers only DRL-based SAN for mobile robots, so imitation learning, inverse RL, and language/vision-language navigation are largely out of scope.
The literature search was limited to three databases and one search string.
